title: “Proprie” means chiefly, not uniquely — covenant faith embraces mysteries too (Rom. 10)
source_text: XCI. Quum vero fides quatenus justificat & salvat, dicitur circa promissiones Evangelii proprie versari, ibi proprie idem significare debet, quod praecipue atque potissimum, non vero idem quod unice. Nec enim fides, quatenus salvat atque justificat, circa promissiones illas unice versatur. Nam fides nos salvare & justificare dicitur, quatenus est conditio foederis gratuiti, quo Deus non amplius a nobis praecise exigit, sub poena aeternae mortis & maledictionis, omnibus suis numeris perfectam & absolutam legis observationem, quod postulabat foedus legale sive operum; sed fidem vivam, & quae per dilectionem operetur. Cum enim lex Mosis diceret, fac & vives, Evangelium dicit, crede & servaberis. Fides autem illa quam postulat Evangelium, ut conditionem sub qua salutem nobis offert, non respicit solas Evangelii promissiones, sed etiam ejus praecepta & dogmata; quale est illud de Resurrectione Jesu Christi Domini nostri, ut manifestum est ex istis Pauli verbis, Quod si confitearis in ore tuo Dominum Jesum, & in corde tuo credideris quod Deus illum suscitavit a mortuis, salvus eris. Corde enim creditur ad justitiam, ore autem fit confessio ad salutem, Rom. 10. Adeoque fides illa, sub cujus conditione, Deus nos propter Christum a peccatis absolvit, & tanquam justos habet, non est ille solus mentis & voluntatis actus quo promissiones gratiae amplectimur, sed etiam ille quo mysteriis Evangelicis, ut veris assentimur. Et idcirco non probamus eos qui videntur objectum fidei qua justificans est, ad promissionem gratiae restringere; licet haec promissio sit praecipuum illius objectum.
pass_a_gloss: But when faith inasmuch as it justifies and saves is said to be properly conversant about the promises of the Gospel, there properly ought to signify the same as chiefly and principally, not the same as uniquely. For neither is faith, inasmuch as it saves and justifies, uniquely conversant about those promises. For faith is said to save and justify us inasmuch as it is the condition of the gracious covenant, by which God no longer precisely exacts from us, under penalty of eternal death and curse, a perfect and absolute observation of the law in all its numbers, which the legal or works-covenant demanded; but a living faith, and one which works through love. For when the law of Moses said, do and you shall live, the Gospel says, believe and you shall be saved. But that faith which the Gospel demands as the condition under which it offers salvation to us does not regard the Gospel promises alone, but also its precepts and dogmas; such as that concerning the Resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord, as is plain from these words of Paul, That if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation, Romans 10. And so that faith under whose condition God absolves us from sins for Christ and holds us as just is not that sole act of mind and will by which we embrace the promises of grace, but also that by which we assent to the Gospel mysteries as true. And therefore we do not approve those who seem to restrict the object of faith as justifying to the promise of grace; although this promise is its chief object.
pass_b_english: “Proprie” here = chiefly/principally, not uniquely — justifying faith is not only about promises.
Faith saves as condition of the gracious covenant (living faith working through love), not as perfect law-keeping.
Moses: do and live; Gospel: believe and be saved — and that faith also covers precepts and dogmas (e.g. the Resurrection).
Rom. 10: heart-belief and mouth-confession — so justifying faith includes assent to Gospel mysteries, not grace-promise alone (though that remains chief).
